subject: Physiology
summary: Gastric Inhibitory Peptide (GIP) is an incretin hormone released from duodenal K‑cells after meals, especially fats and carbs. It suppresses gastric acid secretion and strongly stimulates insulin release in a glucose‑dependent manner, linking digestion to glucose homeostasis.

sections.p: GIP is a 42‑amino‑acid peptide secreted by K‑cells of the proximal small intestine. It rises within minutes of nutrient entry and falls as glucose normalises.
b: Peak plasma levels 5–10 min after a mixed meal
Acts via GIP receptor (a G‑protein‑coupled receptor) on pancreatic β‑cells

sections.p: GIP binds to its receptor on β‑cells, activating adenylate cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A, which potentiates glucose‑stimulated insulin secretion. It also reduces gastric acid and motility, slowing nutrient delivery.
b: Enhances insulin only when plasma glucose > 5 mmol/L
Inhibits gastric acid secretion via somatostatin release
Slows gastric emptying, aiding post‑prandial glucose control

sections.p: Nutrient composition drives GIP release; fats and carbohydrates are potent stimuli, while proteins are weaker. Hyperglycaemia and certain drugs (e.g., DPP‑4 inhibitors) prolong its action.
b: Meal‑induced rise proportional to carbohydrate/fat load
Elevated in obesity, blunted in type 2 diabetes

sections.p: In type 2 diabetes, β‑cell responsiveness to GIP is markedly reduced, contributing to impaired post‑prandial insulin release. Rare GIP‑receptor mutations cause severe hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia.
b: Reduced GIP effect → inadequate insulin after meals
Excessive GIP activity (e.g., rare receptor gain‑of‑function) can cause hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia
GIP levels may be high in obesity but ineffective

sections.p: Understanding GIP helps explain why incretin‑based therapies (GLP‑1 agonists, DPP‑4 inhibitors) improve glycaemic control and why GIP alone is less effective in established type 2 diabetes.
b: GIP contributes to the ‘incretin effect’ – > 50 % of post‑prandial insulin is incretin‑mediated
DPP‑4 inhibitors raise endogenous GIP and GLP‑1 levels
Future dual‑agonists (GIP + GLP‑1) aim to overcome GIP resistance

t.a: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) with insulin measurement
t.b: Does the patient have a blunted insulin response to oral glucose (suggesting impaired incretin effect)? A low insulin rise despite high glucose points to GIP/GLP‑1 resistance.
Is GIP elevated but ineffective? High GIP with poor insulin response supports receptor resistance, common in long‑standing type 2 diabetes.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: GIP is an incretin from K‑cells, stimulates insulin only when glucose is high, and its action is lost early in type 2 diabetes.
b: Stimulates insulin in a glucose‑dependent way
Reduced β‑cell response in type 2 diabetes

whenToSeekHelp: Recurrent hypoglycaemia despite low insulin doses (possible hyper‑GIP activity)
Unexplained persistent vomiting and gastric outlet obstruction

faq.q: Why does GIP not raise insulin when blood glucose is low?
faq.a: Its receptor signalling requires a glucose threshold; without glucose, cAMP cannot trigger insulin granule exocytosis.

faq.q: How does DPP‑4 inhibition affect GIP?
faq.a: DPP‑4 inhibitors prevent GIP degradation, modestly increasing its plasma level and enhancing residual incretin effect.

faq.q: Is GIP the same as GLP‑1?
faq.a: No. Both are incretins, but GLP‑1 is secreted from L‑cells, has stronger insulinotropic and appetite‑suppressing effects, and is the main target of current drugs.

exam: Describe the source, stimulus, and primary actions of Gastric Inhibitory Peptide.
Explain why the incretin effect is reduced in type 2 diabetes, focusing on GIP.
Compare the therapeutic relevance of GIP versus GLP‑1 in modern diabetes treatment.
